• Communication and collaboration: The learner listens keenly to group members and speaks clearly to share information during group activities. In this unit: learners discuss and present findings from breathing-rate and pulse-rate practicals, collaboratively construct and revise gaseous exchange models, and debate the implications of aerobic vs. anaerobic respiration during exercise in Kenyan athletes such as marathon runners from Iten.
• Learning to learn: The learner develops relationships while sharing information with group members. In this unit: learners compare their first models with a partner (Lesson 1), swap models for peer review (Lessons 10-11) and track how their own ideas change on the Driving Question Board.
Also developed in this unit (not listed by KICD for this sub-strand):
• Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: Learners analyse data on respiratory quotients for different food substrates (e.g., maize starch vs. nyama choma fat), identify patterns, and draw evidence-based conclusions about energy metabolism.
• Creativity and Imagination: Learners design and iteratively improve annotated diagrams and physical models of the human respiratory system and alveolar gas-exchange surfaces.
• Digital Literacy: Learners use the ARES offline platform to watch simulations and videos on oxygen transport through the circulatory system and interpret virtual spirometer data.
• Self-Efficacy: Learners develop confidence in conducting and interpreting quantitative practicals (measuring breathing rate, pulse rate, and calculating RQ values) and connecting results to their own lived experience of physical activity.

• Respect: The learner is considerate of others' opinions while working together in groups discussing the adaptations of respiratory sites and structures. In this unit: learners appreciate diverse body responses observed during the breathing-and-pulse practical, recognising that physiological variation is normal and avoiding ridicule of peers' results.
• Responsibility: The learner engages in assigned roles and duties within groups as they search for information on adaptations of respiratory sites. In this unit: learners handle laboratory apparatus (e.g., limewater, thermometers, stopwatches) with care and follow safety protocols during respiration experiments, reflecting responsibility for self and peers.
Also developed in this unit (not listed by KICD for this sub-strand):
• Unity: Learners work collaboratively in mixed-ability groups during model-building and practical activities, valuing each member's contribution to the collective understanding of gaseous exchange.
• Social Justice: Learners discuss how access to clean air and adequate nutrition (e.g., sufficient carbohydrates from ugali and githeri) affects respiratory health, linking biology to equity in Kenyan communities.

records.value:
• Social awareness skills: The learner communicates effectively to peers while working in groups. In this unit: learners share and compare their breathing-rate and pulse-rate results in pairs and groups and respond to each other's data without ridicule.
• Animal welfare: The learner handles the animals humanely during the practical and project activities. In this unit: any specimen (for example tilapia gills in Lesson 3) is handled respectfully, and no live animal is harmed for a lesson.
Also addressed in this unit (not listed by KICD for this sub-strand):
• Health Education: Learners connect efficient gaseous exchange and respiration to personal health choices, including the importance of physical activity and avoiding smoking — a growing public-health concern in urban Kenya (Nairobi, Mombasa).
• Environmental Conservation: Learners examine how air pollution from matatu emissions and industrial activity in Kenyan cities impairs respiratory surfaces, and discuss community responsibility for clean air.
• Safety and Security: Learners follow proper laboratory safety procedures when using limewater (an irritant) and conducting breathing-rate experiments, and learn about dangers of oxygen-deficient environments (e.g., enclosed grain stores in rural Kenya).
• Life Skills Education: Learners develop decision-making and self-management skills by reflecting on how lifestyle factors (diet of carbohydrates from ugali vs. fats from nyama choma, exercise, altitude in the Rift Valley) affect their own rate of respiration and energy availability.
• Financial Literacy: Learners discuss how understanding fermentation (anaerobic respiration in yeast) underpins food-preservation and brewing industries in Kenya, connecting biology to entrepreneurship opportunities.

records.why: The claim that Lake Victoria has less dissolved oxygen than open ocean water is not reliable (fresh water holds slightly MORE oxygen than sea water at the same temperature). The real point for gills is that water holds far less oxygen than air: air is about 21% oxygen (about 210 mL per litre), water at 25 degrees C holds about 8 mg per litre (about 5.6 mL), and 210 / 5.6 = about 37 times; at 15 degrees C about 30 times, so 'roughly 30 times' is a safe statement.
records.old: The water there has less dissolved oxygen than open ocean water — and the fish must keep swimming.
records.new: Water holds far less dissolved oxygen than air (roughly 30 times less per litre), and warm tropical lake water holds even less — and the fish must keep swimming.
records.reference: Campbell Biology, chapter on Gas Exchange (oxygen content of air versus water)

records.old: It happens in the mitochondria. Contracting muscles need much more ATP during step-ups, so aerobic respiration speeds up. It uses more glucose (from food such as ugali) and more oxygen and produces more carbon dioxide. The body therefore has to breathe faster to supply oxygen and remove carbon dioxide. (b) When oxygen delivery to the muscle cells cannot keep up with demand, aerobic respiration alone cannot supply enough ATP. The cells switch to anaerobic respiration, which releases energy without oxygen but gives far less ATP. In animal muscle this produces lactic acid. The acid builds up in the muscle and causes the burning sensation, even though the lungs are working hard. (c) During intense exercise an oxygen debt builds up. Heavy breathing continues afterwards to supply the extra oxygen needed to break down the accumulated lactic acid into carbon dioxide and water.
records.new: The first step (glycolysis) happens in the cytoplasm and the main energy-releasing steps happen in the mitochondria. Contracting muscles need much more ATP during step-ups, so aerobic respiration speeds up. It uses more glucose (from food such as ugali) and more oxygen and produces more carbon dioxide. The extra carbon dioxide makes the blood slightly more acidic; sensors detect this and the breathing centre in the brain (the medulla) sends faster signals to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles, so the body breathes faster to supply oxygen and remove carbon dioxide. (b) When oxygen delivery to the muscle cells cannot keep up with demand, aerobic respiration alone cannot supply enough ATP. The cells switch to anaerobic respiration, which releases energy without oxygen but gives far less ATP. In animal muscle this produces lactic acid: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃ + energy (about 2 ATP). The acid builds up in the muscle and causes the burning sensation, even though the lungs are working hard. (c) During intense exercise an oxygen debt builds up. Heavy breathing continues afterwards to supply the extra oxygen needed to break down the accumulated lactic acid into carbon dioxide and water. (d) RQ = CO₂ produced ÷ O₂ used = 1 400 ÷ 2 000 = 0.70, which means fat is the main food being respired. (e) For example growth, active transport of substances across cell membranes, keeping the body temperature steady, and reproduction.

records.why: The CBE rubric has four levels (Exceeds, Meets, Approaches, Below Expectations) but the data contract allows only three level fields (excellent, proficient, developing), so the printed rubric cannot show a 'Below Expectations' level. Suggestion: ask the partner whether a fourth field can be added, or print a separate Below Expectations descriptor on the teacher marking sheet; this cannot be fixed inside the current contract.

KICD naming mismatch (flag only, not renamed): KICD March 2025 calls Strand 3.0 'Anatomy and Physiology of Animals' and the sub-strand '3.3 Gaseous Exchange and Respiration'. This unit's data says 'Strand 3.0: Physiology of Life Processes' and 'Sub-Strand 3.3: Animal Gaseous Exchange and Respiration'. The numbers (3.0, 3.3) agree. Suggest aligning the strand and sub-strand names with KICD when titles are next regenerated.

records.why: KICD content not taught: the KICD suggested experiences and content name amphibians (lungs, buccal cavity, skin), birds (lungs), insect respiratory siphons and tracheal gills as respiratory structures, and a small-mammal dissection. The unit covers earthworm skin, fish gills, insect tracheae and human alveoli only. Suggest adding amphibians and birds as a 5-minute comparison in Lesson 3 (or as a Lesson 11 extension), if time allows; Lesson 3 is already tight after trimming.

Resource check (guideline 11): the Lesson 4 ARES animation is described as showing a pressure change of about 101 kPa to 99 kPa. If the actual animation shows numbers of that size they are about 15 times too large (real quiet breathing changes lung pressure by about 0.1 kPa). Please check the animation; if it shows 99 kPa, tell learners it is exaggerated for clarity or choose another animation.
